title: Yom Kippur: Neilah, lived
hookLine: the last hour, when the gates close; many stand the whole time
tomorrow: how small can a sukkah be and still count?

cards: The last two minutes of a close game. Final boarding at the gate. The lights flickering in a store about to close.
Something changes in people when a door is about to shut. Yom Kippur ends on that feeling and gives it a name: Neilah. Locking.
The last service of the day, as the light goes. And the rabbis couldn't agree on what exactly is being locked.

teach.b: In the Jerusalem Talmud, Rav says the gates of heaven. Rabbi Yochanan says the gates of the Temple, shut at the end of the day. Either way, gates, and an hour.
Neilah is a service you take in with the whole body. What you see: the ark, the cabinet that holds the Torah scrolls, opened.
In some synagogues it stays open the whole hour, and some people stand the whole time, tired, hungry, upright. What you hear: one word changes in the prayers.
All season people have asked to be written in the book of life; now they ask to be sealed. What you feel: the emptiness of a day without food, and the light going out of the windows. Then the end.
The room says the first line of the Shema together, and then "The LORD, He is God," again and again, the cry the people give in Elijah's story on Mount Carmel.
And then one long blast of the shofar. The fast ends on a sound. The idea under all of it is simple.
The last hour isn't what's left over after the real day. It's where the day is sealed. Whatever you have left, it goes here.

how: Neilah is the closing service of Yom Kippur, prayed as the sun sets; the ark is often left open and some stand throughout, and the day ends with the Shema, 'The LORD, He is God,' and a long blast of the shofar.

games.q: it's the last hour of a long day of fasting, and you're wiped out. the ark opens for Neilah. what fits the hour?
o: sit out the end; you already did the hard part of the day.
stand if you can, and give the last hour what you have left.
slip out early to beat the line at the break-fast table.
games.why: Neilah treats the last hour as the point: the ark open, the book being sealed, one long note to close.

practice: For the sit, stand up if you can, or sit tall at the very edge of your chair. Feet flat, hands open, palms up, like an ark with its doors wide. Stay there, and let it take a little effort, the way the last hour does.
If something from this season is still unsaid, a thanks or a sorry, let it come to mind while you hold the posture.
